prerequisites.title: SurveyMonkey developer account
prerequisites.detail: Any SurveyMonkey account works for the developer of a public app; confirm the plan for a private app.

prerequisites.title: English app listing and support
prerequisites.detail: The first listing must be in English and you must offer easy support. State if users need a free or paid account from you.

prerequisites.title: HTTPS with valid certificate
prerequisites.detail: All app communication must use HTTPS with a valid SSL certificate.

steps.title: Register the app in the developer console
steps.detail: Log in to SurveyMonkey and register an app. This makes a draft with a token for your own account.
steps.done_when: You have a client ID and secret.

steps.title: Create Composio auth config
steps.detail: Create the auth config via Composio's API with your client ID and secret. Copy the redirect URI from the Composio dashboard into the SurveyMonkey app.
steps.done_when: Auth config exists and a test connection works.

steps.title: Draft listing and scope justifications
steps.detail: Write an honest English listing, state the account requirement and support details, and check the app name rules.
steps.done_when: Listing draft is ready for review.

steps.title: Submit the listing for approval
steps.detail: Use the listings tab in My Apps to create and submit the listing.

steps.title: Wait for SurveyMonkey approval
steps.detail: No review time is documented. Deploy before the 90-day draft ends.
steps.done_when: The app is approved and deployed.

traps.title: Draft apps are disabled after 90 days
traps.detail: Only your own account can authenticate a draft, and it is disabled if not deployed within 90 days.

traps.title: Low draft rate limits
traps.detail: Draft and private apps start at 120 calls per minute and 500 per day. Going over 100% three times in 30 days triggers enforcement.

traps.title: Two scopes need separate approval
traps.detail: Create/Modify Responses and Create/Modify Surveys need SurveyMonkey approval even in a public app.

traps.title: Approval can be refused
traps.detail: SurveyMonkey may reject an app on criteria not listed, and approval does not guarantee compliance.

blockers.symptom: Other accounts cannot authorize the app
blockers.what_it_means: The app is a draft or private, so only one account or Team has access.
blockers.what_to_do: Build a public app and submit it for approval.
blockers.agent_can_help: Prepare the listing and review the checklist.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: | [SurveyMonkey](/toolkits/survey_monkey.md) | `SURVEY_MONKEY` |
evidence.answer: SurveyMonkey is listed under the 'Bring your own OAuth app' section, not the Composio-managed section, so Composio does not supply a managed OAuth app for it on this page.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: ## Bring your own OAuth app (219)
evidence.answer: The page places the 'Bring your own OAuth app' list under a heading that counts 219 toolkits, which includes SurveyMonkey.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: If the field does not contain that method, register your own OAuth app and supply its client ID and client secret.
evidence.answer: For a toolkit whose OAuth method is not Composio-managed, the developer must register their own OAuth app and supply its client ID and client secret.

evidence.question: G1
evidence.quote: SurveyMonkey account needed by Developer
evidence.answer: For Public apps, the developer's SurveyMonkey account requirement is listed as 'Any'. For Private apps it is listed as 'Sign In to View Plan'.

evidence.question: G2
evidence.quote: Requires approval before launching
evidence.answer: Public apps require approval before launching (the page's comparison table, Public Apps column).

evidence.question: G2
evidence.quote: Eligible for the App Directory
evidence.answer: Public apps are eligible for the App Directory; Private apps are not.

evidence.question: G2
evidence.quote: How many accounts can access the app
evidence.answer: Private apps are limited to one SurveyMonkey account or one Team, while Public apps have unlimited accounts that can access the app.

evidence.question: G4
evidence.quote: Public app developers should understand which scopes they'll need.
evidence.answer: The page says public app developers should understand which scopes they will need, and points to the API Documentation for more on scopes; it does not list specific scopes or which need extra review.

evidence.question: G7
evidence.quote: If you're building a Private app and think you need a higher API limit you should reach out to our sales team .
evidence.answer: For Private apps, a developer who needs a higher API limit should contact the SurveyMonkey sales team to purchase more API calls.

evidence.question: G8
evidence.quote: Plan needed to utilize app functionality
evidence.answer: For Public apps, the SurveyMonkey user must be an end user of the app to use its functionality, and the End User (not the developer) purchases the user's SurveyMonkey accounts.

evidence.question: G8
evidence.quote: Who purchases user's SM accounts
evidence.answer: For Public apps the end user purchases the user's SurveyMonkey accounts; for Private apps the developer purchases them.

evidence.question: G10
evidence.quote: You can refresh your app's credential in the settings for your app in the developer portal .
evidence.answer: The developer can refresh the app's credential (secret) in the settings for the app in the developer portal.

evidence.question: G10
evidence.quote: If you're looking for more info on either camp, visit Creating a Public App or Creating a Private App .
evidence.answer: The page refers developers to separate guides for creating a Public app or a Private app.

evidence.question: G11
evidence.quote: Please see our API Developer Terms for more guidelines when building with our API.
evidence.answer: Public app usage is subject to the SurveyMonkey API Developer Terms, which give guidelines for building with the API.

evidence.question: G9
evidence.quote: In your OAuth app's settings, set the authorized redirect URI to your own endpoint:
evidence.answer: When you proxy the redirect through your own domain, the OAuth app's authorized redirect URI is set to your own endpoint.

evidence.question: G9
evidence.quote: https://yourdomain.com/api/composio-redirect
evidence.answer: The example authorized redirect URI for the proxy setup is an endpoint on your own domain.

evidence.question: G9
evidence.quote: This endpoint receives the OAuth callback and immediately 302-redirects it to Composio:
evidence.answer: The proxy endpoint on your domain receives the OAuth callback and immediately redirects it to Composio's callback URL.

evidence.question: G9
evidence.quote: Your endpoint must return a **302 redirect**. Do not follow the redirect server-side or make a fetch call to Composio. The user's browser needs to be redirected so the OAuth flow completes correctly.
evidence.answer: Your proxy endpoint must return a 302 redirect, and must not follow the redirect server-side or fetch Composio itself.

evidence.question: G9
evidence.quote: During OAuth, the browser briefly redirects through `backend.composio.dev` so Composio can capture the auth token.
evidence.answer: During OAuth the browser briefly redirects through Composio's backend domain so Composio can capture the auth token.

evidence.question: G9
evidence.quote: Some toolkits also display this URL on the consent screen.
evidence.answer: Some toolkits display Composio's callback URL on the consent screen.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: "Composio wants to access your account" on Google, GitHub, etc.
evidence.answer: By default the provider consent screen shows 'Composio wants to access your account' (Composio's identity) on providers such as Google and GitHub.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Add your own OAuth app only for toolkits where the provider consent screen must show your brand.
evidence.answer: Composio's hosted flow supplies its own app by default; you should bring your own OAuth app only for toolkits where the provider consent screen must show your brand.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: composio_url = "https://backend.composio.dev/api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback"
evidence.answer: The callback URL on Composio's side that the redirect proxy forwards to is the Composio toolkit auth callback endpoint on backend.composio.dev.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Composio registers and maintains OAuth apps for popular toolkits such as GitHub, Gmail, and Slack. You do not need to register your own OAuth app.
evidence.answer: Composio registers and maintains its own OAuth apps for popular toolkits such as GitHub, Gmail, and Slack (general, not SurveyMonkey-specific), so the developer does not need to register one.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Managed apps are the default when they are available.
evidence.answer: Composio managed apps are the default when they are available.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: You provide your own OAuth app, API key, bearer token, or other credentials and tell Composio to use them for a toolkit.
evidence.answer: A custom auth config lets the developer supply their own OAuth app (or other credentials) for a toolkit and tell Composio to use them.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Users will see "Composio wants to access your account" during OAuth.
evidence.answer: With a Composio managed app, users see 'Composio wants to access your account' on the OAuth consent screen instead of the developer's app name.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Managed apps share quota across all Composio users. Your own app gets a dedicated quota.
evidence.answer: Composio managed apps share their quota across all Composio users; a developer's own app gets a dedicated quota.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Managed auth enforces a 15-minute minimum polling interval; your own app can use shorter polling intervals where supported.
evidence.answer: Managed auth enforces a 15-minute minimum polling interval for triggers; a developer's own app can use shorter polling intervals where supported.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Composio requests sensible defaults for each toolkit.
evidence.answer: Composio managed apps request sensible default scopes for each toolkit, which may not include every scope a developer needs.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Composio's default scopes may not include everything you need (e.g., write access to a specific Google API).
evidence.answer: Composio's default scopes may not include everything a developer needs, for example write access to a specific Google API, so custom scopes may require the developer's own app.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Self-hosted or regional variants (e.g., a private Salesforce subdomain) need their own OAuth app.
evidence.answer: Self-hosted or regional variants of an app (for example a private Salesforce subdomain) need their own OAuth app.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Enterprise customers require your branding end-to-end.
evidence.answer: Enterprise customers who require the developer's branding end-to-end are a listed reason to switch from managed to custom apps.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: You can still create a custom auth config for branding, scopes, rate limits, polling intervals, or custom instances.
evidence.answer: A developer can still create a custom auth config for branding, scopes, rate limits, polling intervals, or custom instances even when a managed app exists.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: You don't have to pick one approach for all toolkits.
evidence.answer: Managed and custom approaches can be mixed: a developer can use their own credentials for some toolkits and Composio managed auth for others, with each toolkit getting its own auth config.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: Each toolkit gets its own auth config independently.
evidence.answer: Each toolkit gets its own auth config independently.

evidence.question: C1
evidence.quote: To check whether Composio provides the OAuth app for a toolkit, see [Managed OAuth apps](/toolkits/managed-auth).
evidence.answer: Whether Composio provides the OAuth app for a given toolkit is checked on the separate Managed OAuth apps page.

evidence.answer: Public apps are the kind that can be listed on the App Directory; the page says public apps have different guidelines than private apps.
